title: ACME Incident Postmortem - Follow-up
summary: 30-minute follow-up on last week’s incident where Acme experienced a partial outage of Redwood-hosted inference causing elevated latencies and 5xx errors for a subset of routes. Discussed root cause, mitigations implemented, longer-term reliability improvements, and next steps for an agreed pilot around dedicated capacity and improved autoscaling rules.
transcript: [00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time on short notice.
[00:06] Maya: No problem. We wanted to go over the fixes you pushed and confirm timelines for the follow-ups.

[00:12] Sofia: Yeah, quick recap from our side first: root cause of last Tuesday's incident was a hot shard on the KV cache plus an autoscaler threshold that didn't react fast enough when we had a burst of long-context requests.
[00:25] Ravi: Just to add, the burst came from a background job that suddenly sent many 4k token requests; our dashboards show queueing on the GPU nodes and then cascading 502s from the gateway.

[00:37] Jordan: Right and we saw compounding issues because the fallback policy was configured to a model variant that was incompatible for the payload size, so the graceful degradation didn't trigger cleanly.

[00:49] Jon: For security context, while data didn't leave the VPC, our compliance team wants the audit logs and timeline for forensics; we need showback for the execs around who accessed what and when.

[00:58] Sofia: We can provide the audit export; Redwood logs include token-level traces and request ids. There may be some mislabelled fields in the auto-translated logs but we will validate them with you.
[01:10] Maya: Could you explain the KV cache hot-shard a bit more? I'm not fully following how it caused the latency to spike.

[01:17] Sofia: Sure. So our runtime uses prefix/KV caching to avoid recomputing prefixes for repeated prompts. In this case, because of the background job pattern, a small subset of keys got reused heavily causing memory pressure on one mobile of the KV store -- I mean one node, sorry, and the request routing concentrated there. The node started thrashing its cache and the eviction behavior caused longer tail LRU misses.
[01:35] Ravi: Was the underlying issue the cache size, or the routing policy?

[01:39] Sofia: Both. Cache size on that pool was tuned for typical traffic; the routing policy favored throughput and put more traffic on the same GPU shard to reduce cross-node KV lookups, which backfired under that traffic pattern.
[01:51] Jordan: Quick note: during the incident we temporarily changed autoscaler thresholds and added a manual flush to the cache which helped bring latency down within 12 minutes.
[01:59] Maya: Yeah we noticed the spike lasted ~20 minutes in our metrics; thanks for the quick mitigation, but we need a plan to prevent recurrence.

[02:06] Sofia: Agreed. Short term we implemented an autoscaler policy tweak (lower CPU/latency thresholds) and added a fallback route to a faster, lower-context model variant that will accept the payload. Long-term we recommend dedicated pool + tuned routing for heavy workloads.
[02:20] Ravi: There was also some confusion with the retry behavior. Our client retried aggressively and that multiplied the load. Any guidance for clients?
[02:28] Jordan: We're adding a guidance doc for exponential backoff and sticky request ids; we'll share that. Also recommending client-side rate limits for background jobs.
[02:35] Jon: From security, we need the timeline and the audit export by EOD Tuesday for the compliance review. Can that be done?
[02:42] Jordan: Yes. We'll produce the audit logs and a compact timeline. Sofia, can you own that?
[02:47] Sofia: Yep, I'll pull the request traces and annotate them. There may be small gaps in the auto-generated field names but we'll cross-check with gateway ids.
[02:56] Maya: About dedicated capacity -- cost is a concern. Can we do a pilot that only moves the most critical routes?

[03:03] Sofia: Absolutely. We can start with a single dedicated pool for your payment and checkout routes and keep everything else on hosted. That gives isolation and predictable latency for critical paths.
[03:11] Ravi: How long to stand up a dedicated pool?
[03:13] Jordan: For a pilot we can have it provisioned in ~7 business days once we agree on capacity and commit. If you need a hardened on-prem setup that adds more lead time.
[03:21] Maya: We also want SLA targets and rollback plans for deploys. Your console mentioned canary rollouts and automatic fallbacks?

[03:28] Sofia: Yes, Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, automatic fallback to a model variant, and per-route tracing. We also have a rollout policy that will automatically divert traffic if latency exceeds thresholds.
[03:37] Ravi: On telemetry, can you increase retention for the last 30 days of trace data for our team to do deeper analysis?
[03:43] Jordan: We can enable extended retention on the account as an add-on; we'll send pricing for that.
[03:47] Maya: Any immediate code changes we should make client-side?
[03:50] Sofia: Add exponential backoff, avoid parallelizing the same long-context request, and add request size validation to reject unintentional 4k payloads from background jobs.
[03:59] Jon: Also, we asked about KMS: were any keys rotated or affected?
[04:03] Sofia: No KMS keys were affected. All keys are customer controlled in the VPC/private deployment. For hosted accounts the KMS integration is via customer-managed keys where configured.

[04:12] Jordan: Recap of root cause: traffic pattern created KV cache hot-shard + autoscaler thresholds too high + client retries amplified load. Mitigation: manual cache flush & lowered autoscaler thresholds during incident; follow-ups include dedicated pool pilot, routing tweaks, and client guidance.
[04:26] Maya: Okay sounds good. Can you enumerate the next steps and owners?
[04:30] Jordan: Yep, we'll do that. Sofia will deliver logs and annotated timeline; Jordan will send pricing and pilot agreement; RavI will validate client changes on their side.
[04:41] Ravi: Small note, in the timeline doc please map request ids back to our internal job ids if possible, that makes troubleshooting faster.
[04:48] Sofia: We can map gateway ids to request ids and provide a guidance table, will need your mapping table.
[04:54] Maya: Good. Any other concerns?

[04:57] Jordan: One more: we noticed some references to competitor services during the incident review; just to be transparent, customers sometimes ask about moving to OpenAI endpoints or Bedrock for redundancy. There are tradeoffs on cost and custom model support.
[05:10] Maya: Noted. For now we prefer Redwood if we can get predictable latency on critical routes.
[05:14] Jordan: Great. Let's align on dates: Sofia, can you commit to audit logs + annotated timeline by 2025-04-15?
[05:24] Jordan: I will send pricing and pilot agreement by 2025-04-14. Ravi, can your team make the client-side change and report back by 2025-04-18?
[05:33] Ravi: Yes we'll target 2025-04-18 for the client patch and validations.
[05:37] Maya: Thanks everyone, that covers our asks. We appreciate the quick support and the proposed mitigations.
[05:43] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with the items and links. End call.
[45:00] <call ended>
next_steps: Sofia to deliver audit logs and annotated incident timeline by 2025-04-15
Jordan to send dedicated pool pilot pricing and agreement by 2025-04-14
Acme to implement client-side exponential backoff and request size validation by 2025-04-18
Redwood to propose autoscaler/routing config for pilot and share runbook
